blocks.md: Suppose an iterative search policy resolves more connection-pool failures than a single-call baseline. That gain might come from the search algorithm itself, or it might come from a larger token budget, a stronger base model, or silently dropping timed-out tasks from the denominator.

questions.q: The section **Evaluating Deliberation Policies** develops one of the chapter's claims. Which one?
options: The precision of a passing verdict depends on the valid-candidate base rate and the check's error rates, not on pool size, so a larger pool raises both the chance of a selection and the chance of a false pass.
Recording a candidate as a dependency graph of artifacts with evidence provenance lets a refuting observation invalidate exactly its descendants while retained branches keep their support.
A step check that rejects a fraction r of b children gives an effective branching factor b(1-r), so a tree stays finite on its own only when r > 1-1/b and otherwise needs hard caps.
Voting and learned ranking both return the best failure from a defective pool, so only selection by a check the candidate cannot modify justifies returning a candidate instead of abstaining.
